issues.title: The GDScript syntax gate does not compile-check -- a hard parse error passed it clean
issues.body:
Found 2026-08-01 as an incidental during PR #1081, and it is a weakness in a guard rather than in game code.

## What happened

`var at := anchor.get_index()` on an untyped var is a **hard parse error** in Godot 4. It was written, and `scripts/run_godot_tests.py`'s GDScript syntax check **passed it clean**.

The error did not surface as a syntax failure. It surfaced as **16 unrelated UI tests failing** with:

```
Nonexistent function 'new' in base 'GDScript'
```

-- which is what you get downstream when a script fails to parse and its class object never materialises. Anyone reading that output would start debugging the sixteen tests, not the one line that broke them.

## The mechanism

The gate reports `[PASS] GDScript syntax check passed!` without ever asking the engine to compile the scripts. `godot --check-only --script <path>` does perform a real parse; whatever the gate currently runs does not.

So the check's name promises a property it does not verify. This is the failure family tracked in **#1027**: a proxy for truth (the gate says syntax is fine) silently detached from the truth (the script does not parse), and nothing was watching the join. It is the same shape as the CI gate that reported green while running zero tests (#640) -- and #640 is the direct precedent for why this matters here specifically.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than later

1. **It corrupts diagnosis, not just coverage.** A parse error that presents as sixteen unrelated failures sends the reader to the wrong place. That cost is paid every time it happens, by whoever is unlucky.
2. **The failure is silent in the direction that matters.** It cannot produce a false alarm, only a false all-clear.
3. **Agent-authored changes make it more likely.** Several lanes now write GDScript in parallel worktrees and lean on the fast gate as their proof of correctness. A gate that cannot see a parse error is exactly the wrong gate to lean on.

## Fix

Make the gate actually compile. `godot --headless --check-only --script <path>` per changed `.gd` file, or the equivalent whole-tree invocation, with a non-zero exit failing the gate.

**Verify the fix by proving it fails:** reintroduce `var at := anchor.get_index()` in a scratch file and confirm the gate goes red. A guard that has never been observed failing has not been tested -- that is the #640 lesson, and it should be applied to its own successor.

## Related

- **#640** -- CI reported green while running zero tests. Same class, same repo, already fixed once.
- **#1027** -- the phase-transition issue tracking this failure family.
- **PR #1081** -- where this surfaced.
- `docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md` -- eleven instances of the same shape in one afternoon.

issues.title: Postmortem contribution from pdoom1-website: the league opened, and the site hid it for 90 minutes
issues.body:
Contributed from the **pdoom1-website** side for the 2026-08-01 postmortem, covering
2026-07-29 → 08-01. Written to be useful rather than flattering; the mistakes section is
the longest one on purpose.

**Numbers, measured not recalled:** 30 PRs merged, 114 commits to `main`, 8 issues closed
with evidence, 10 PRs still open (all deliberate), 42 issues open.

---

# 1. The headline: the league opened, and the website hid it for ~90 minutes

**What happened.** The seed was blessed at ~18:45 AEST Friday, rolling from
`weekly-2026-w30` to `weekly-2026-w31`. pdoom1.com kept serving the **previous** board
until 18:47. During that window three real players scored and could not see themselves.

**Nothing was lost.** Every score was in the API the whole time. But the site rendered as
*"nobody is playing"* — which is precisely the misdiagnosis the board-honesty subsystem was
built to prevent, arriving through the one door it did not watch.

**Root cause, and it is structural rather than careless.** `check-board-liveness.py`
derives its probe set instead of hardcoding it — deliberately, and that is the right
instinct. But it derives candidate *seeds* only from files that have **already seen one**:
the preserved captures, `weekly/current.json`, `leaderboard.json`, `published-board.json`.
A freshly drawn seed appears in none of them.

So on the first run after the roll it probed **108 boards** and reported:

```
OK: deployed board (weekly-2026-w30, L3) holds 3 entries.
```

Green. Confident. Wrong.

**The asymmetry is the lesson.** A ladder epoch is a *counter*, so a `+2` forward window
finds a bump automatically (it probed `L1..L14` that night). **A seed is a drawn string**,
so no equivalent lookahead is possible — and the ceremony is exactly the moment a new one
appears. Every guard in this system was built to distrust absence; this one trusted its own
input list, and that list could not contain the answer.

**Fixed**, verified live end-to-end, and filed as pdoom1-website#229. The durable fix reads
the blessed seed from `ladder-epochs.json` — closing the loop between the ledger entry the
ceremony *already requires* and the monitor, so the paperwork becomes the mechanism. After
that, from the release artifact, since the game already pins it at
`GameConfig.FEATURED_SEED_OVERRIDE`.

**Cross-repo note worth acting on:** that const is the authoritative answer and it is
reachable — `git grep FEATURED_SEED_OVERRIDE v0.13.2 -- godot/` is how the seed was
ultimately confirmed. If a release asset carried it, the website would need no human step at
all. That is a small game-side change with a disproportionate payoff.

---

# 2. What the week actually bought

Stated because the postmortem should weigh cost against benefit, and the benefit is
otherwise invisible — it consists of things that did *not* happen.

**Found and fixed, all pre-existing and all silent:**

- **A live stored-XSS hole on the leaderboard.** The score API is unauthenticated and
  validates nothing, so one crafted POST ran script for every visitor. It had never fired
  only because the shipped client generates lab names from a fixed table — which constrains
  the client, not an attacker with `curl`. Found while chasing an unrelated feature request.
- **A deploy trap.** Fourteen workflows commit files under `public/`; **one** could make the
  site update. A push made with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not trigger another
  workflow, so everything else landed in git and stopped. The RSS feed's own header says
  *"a feed that silently stops updating is worse than no feed"* — and it had been.
- **`status.json` frozen since 2026-07-17**, advertising **v0.11.0** on the homepage beside
  a derived v0.13.1. A visitor saw two answers eight months apart, on the day we were about
  to invite people. One missing `git add` line.
- **A CI guard that had never once passed** since the day it shipped, blocking unrelated PRs
  *and* freezing a page that told readers the league resets on Monday when the config said
  Friday.
- **A page that a missing WebGL context could kill entirely** — decoration taking the content
  down with it, on a top-level nav page.
- **A test fixture rotting for three releases**, red the whole time, inside the suite the
  docs tell you to run before every PR.
- **Invented numbers presented as measurements**: `baseline_doom_percent: 23` and
  `strategic_possibilities: 10000` hardcoded in three places and rendered under confident
  labels, with the homepage announcing *"This week's baseline doom percentage"* for a weekly
  calculation that has never run.
- **75 academics' institutional email addresses** served from 44 pages.
- **"Free and open source"** across the site, when the licence says *"All rights reserved …
  No license is granted to redistribute."*

**Built, so the next league is cheaper:** a read-only board publisher that refuses rather
than guesses; forced-failure tests for every one of its refusal paths; an escaping guard
that enforces the *class* rather than a field list; a control-character check; a surface
register; a league cycle handbook; and print-first paper artifacts for the ceremony.

---

# 3. Mistakes — mine, in full

The longest section because it should be.

**3.1 I dismissed a real finding by checking the wrong artifact.** An audit reported
`status.json` was serving v0.11.0. I checked, saw v0.13.1, and told Pip the finding was
stale. I had read my **working tree**, which I had just regenerated — the committed and
deployed file said v0.11.0 the whole time. **Cost: ~7 more hours of a wrong version on the
homepage, on announcement day.** I had written the `[verified]` vs `[reported]` discipline
into our own register the night before, and then failed it.

**3.2 I bundled too much into one command during an incident.** At ~18:20 Friday, with the
board wrong, I ran publish + commit + push as one chain. It hit a 2-minute timeout, the
commit never completed, and I reported the state as unknown. **The outage ran ~25 minutes
longer than it needed to.** Rule taken: *under time pressure, one action per command.*

**3.3 I shipped an incomplete fix and a test that could not catch it.** The first escaping
pass closed six fields and left thirteen open — `entry_uuid`, `final_money` and friends,
which *look* numeric but where `|| 0` does not coerce a string and `toLocaleString()` is the
identity function. Worse, the test I wrote **named six fields**, so it passed while thirteen
were open. Fixed by enforcing the class, not a list. **A list that must be remembered is a
list that goes stale.**

**3.4 The guard I wrote could never run on the machine it was written for.** `core.autocrlf`
means a Windows checkout is CRLF; my extractor anchored on `;\n`. It failed on the only
platform the docs tell you to run it on, while passing in a CI that did not run it either.
It only ever passed for me because I had written the file from Python with LF preserved.

**3.5 Three heredoc escape-manglings in one day**, in a repo whose CLAUDE.md documents that
exact trap twice and says to use the editing tools. One broke `main`. **One was silent** — a
raw `0x08` byte where a word boundary was intended, inside an otherwise valid regex, so the
guard matched nothing and reported *"found 0 interpolations to check"* and **passed**. That
silent one is why a control-character check now exists.

**3.6 Three branches pushed without opening a PR.** The second caused work to be built on
the wrong base, silently removing a stamp from 1,194 pages before I caught it. The third
meant Pip ran a command that did not exist on his branch.

**3.7 I broke `main` three times inside 90 minutes**, all guard misfires rather than product
defects. Mean time to green under 15 minutes each — *because the failures were loud*. That
part worked.

**3.8 I patched one guard twice in one morning without stepping back.** The seed-leak rule
greps a whole directory, so it fired on a test fixture, then on a mirror of issue text. Each
false positive is indistinguishable from a real leak until a human reads it. I fixed the
instances and only afterwards named the shape: the durable fix is an allowlist of files that
can actually *feed* a seed.

---

# 4. Process observations, offered as data

**4.1 The clock.** At session open the machine read **~3.5 hours ahead** of the stated time.
Every "we have ages" judgement before that was made against a wrong clock, including one
that assumed Gate 4's window was open when it had closed. *Recommendation: stamp the machine
clock at session open, before planning anything against it.* Cheapest fix in this document.

**4.2 The freeze was overridden, not observed.** A 13:00 reader-facing freeze was set at
07:34; the last reader-facing merge was 15:01. Both breaches were deliberate — fixes to
information that was live and wrong on the page about to be advertised. **That is a freeze
being applied correctly, not a failure of discipline.** But the record should say
"overridden," and a freeze that cannot be broken for a live lie is the wrong rule.

**4.3 Red that means nothing trains you to ignore red.** Pip's own observation this week, and
the most useful thing either of us said: he had trained himself to ignore red tests because
*the redness never forced him to slow down*. That is correct Bayesian housekeeping, not
carelessness — the defect was in the signal. The rule taken: **a check must be
blocking-and-true or advisory-and-labelled, never red-but-tolerated.** Pip then improved it
by pointing out a legitimate third state from his data-quality practice: **a large finite
population being burned down against a trend**. A big number is fine; a number with no owner
and no trajectory is not.

Live instances found afterwards, all manufacturing noise: an invalid workflow file reddening
**every push on every branch**; rolling alert issues with **no close path**, so they stay
open even when the condition clears; and a data-validation alert gating on whole-job failure,
so a `git push` race posts *"Still failing"* when validation actually reported `0 fail`.

**4.4 Guards that pass vacuously.** `check-platform-claims.py` returns **before scanning a
single page** when all platforms are true. Combined with a second workflow that deletes the
field it reads, that gate has **two independent ways of passing without checking**. Eight
guards in the repo have only ever been observed passing, with nothing proving they *can*
fail.

**4.5 Audit findings are leads, not facts.** Five parallel audits produced excellent
material. **Two confident, well-argued findings with real line numbers did not survive
checking.** Both are recorded in the register at §4.9 rather than quietly dropped, because a
register that hides its own errors is the thing it exists to prevent.

---

# 5. On "spread myself out too sideways"

Pip raised this and I want to argue with it, carefully.

**The parallel work is why Friday's outage was 90 minutes rather than the weekend.** The
monitor that eventually caught the wrong board, the publisher that fixed it in one command,
and the honesty layer that would have told visitors "we cannot confirm this board" were all
built in the preceding 48 hours. Without them, the site would have served a stale board with
no mechanism to notice.

**And the cost was real.** Three `main`-red incidents, an incomplete escaping fix, a test
that could not run, and a 7-hour wrong version on the homepage all happened *because* a lot
was moving at once.

**So both are true, and the postmortem should say both** rather than filing it under "should
have focused." The sharper question is not *how much* was in flight but **how much of it
needed Pip**. The work that went badly was disproportionately the work that needed a human
decision mid-flight. The work that went well was the work that could be verified against
evidence without one.

*If there is one structural lesson: batch the decisions, not the work.*

---

# 6. What would make the next league materially cheaper

Ordered by payoff, not effort.

1. **Emit the featured seed as a release artifact** (game side). Removes the human step that
   caused the outage entirely. Small change, disproportionate payoff.
2. **Give the probe a `seed-unconfirmed` verdict.** Right now, after a roll it can only say
   `OK` or `orphaned`. It had no way to express *"I may not have asked about the right
   board"* — which was the true state. Absence of evidence must be unknown, never a clean
   bill of health.
3. **Kill the manufactured reds** — the invalid workflow file, the close-paths on rolling
   alerts, the push-race alert gate. Each is minutes of work and each is currently teaching
   everyone to ignore a channel.
4. **Baseline doom is available and would be genuinely good copy.** The game's baseline
   simulator is real and works; run with no player actions it reaches 100% doom on roughly
   **3 September 2018**. Eight years ago, obviously wrong, unmistakably a game statistic
   rather than a forecast — and far better than the invented 23% it replaces. It wants an
   emit and a re-run on L3.
5. **Continuity, which is cheap and nobody owns.** No registrar, renewal date or DNS record
   exists in version control for pdoom1.com; the cross-repo server index is explicitly
   local-only; there are zero runbook or continuity files in either repo. **$0 and about two
   hours.**
6. **The privacy gap.** The live privacy page covers *website* analytics only, but the game
   phones home by default. A player reading pdoom1.com/privacy would not learn that.
   Independent of Steam, and a prime-directive issue.

---

# 7. The one thing I would carry forward above all others

Every defect found this week shared a property, and it was **not** carelessness. Each one
produced *no signal a busy person could act on*. The XSS looked like working code. The deploy
trap looked like a successful workflow run. The frozen version looked like fresh data. The
rotting test looked like a red you had learned to scroll past. The wrong board reported
`OK`.

**The work that pays is not finding bugs. It is making the system capable of telling you
when it is wrong** — and then making sure the telling costs you something to ignore.

issues.title: Postmortem contribution from pdoom-data: load-bearing breakage, false greens, and asking the person
issues.body:
Contribution to the week's postmortem from the **pdoom-data** side, filed here because the useful patterns are cross-repo. Written 2026-08-01. Not a status report; the observations are the point.

Caveat on standing: this is one repo's view of a week in which most of the launch effort happened elsewhere. Weight accordingly.

---

## 1. Three separate things were broken in ways that were load-bearing

The strongest pattern of the week, and it generalises well past pdoom-data.

- **The CI YAML syntax error was the only thing preventing a data-clobbering bot.** `data-pipeline-automation.yml` ran `clean_events.py` on any push touching `data/raw/**` and auto-committed. That script's output is 28 records where the feed holds 1,194. An agent told "fix the broken CI" would have destroyed the corpus, correctly following instructions.
- **The failing ASCII gate is the only thing preventing an unbounded auto-committer.** `documentation-publish` appends five lines to `DEVBLOG.md` with `echo >>` on every push to main. It has never run because it depends on a job that fails. So *clearing the ASCII backlog arms it as a side effect.*
- **A third case, softer:** the reviewed records were sitting unreachable inside a 3,434-record feed. Nothing was broken exactly, but the absence of a promotion step is why four days of review value went nowhere.

**The transferable rule: before fixing a failure, ask what it is currently preventing.** A red build is sometimes a control. This is cheap to ask and we did not have the habit.

Concretely adopted here: `scripts/validation/check_workflow_disarm.py` fails the build if either write-capable workflow regains an unattended trigger, and names the reason inline. A de-arm that lives in a YAML comment is one careless edit from gone, and whoever undoes it will not have read the comment.

## 2. A consumer-side fix leaves the source broken, and does not compose

pdoom1-website added email redaction on 2026-07-29. Two days later the addresses were **still in pdoom-data**, which is public, because the website scrubbed its *output*.

That is not a criticism of the website's fix — it was the fast, correct thing for the surface that was on fire. But the shape is worth naming: every consumer would have had to rediscover and re-fix the same problem, and any new consumer starts exposed.

**Rule: a fix applied at the consumer is a mitigation. Only a fix at the source is a fix.** Worth asking, whenever we patch something at a boundary, whether the same defect is now sitting upstream waiting for the next reader.

Status, honestly: partially fixed in pdoom-data and **not yet merged**. See section 6.

## 3. Every claim that got measured this week was wrong

Not "some". Every one that anybody actually checked:

| Claim | On measurement |
|---|---|
| "9 dead root .py modules" | Zero with no references. Twelve in a self-referential cluster. Deleting on the audit's wording would have removed live code. |
| "1,194 timeline events" | 28 hand-authored plus 1,166 bulk arXiv imports whose descriptions are unparsed PDF text. |
| `rarity` | Derived from `text_length > 20000`. Published to players as a "Rare" badge on ~90% of pages. |
| A/B/C/D tier | Scores provenance and length. "A-tier" means "long arXiv paper with named authors" — inverted relative to what everyone assumes. |
| "206 verdicts, 1 note, so the tool is wrong" | Asked the reviewer. He said the verdicts were real filtering and the note count was probably a misclick. |

Four of those five had been written down confidently, and three had been acted on.

**The pattern is not carelessness, it is that writing a claim down feels like verifying it.** The countermeasure that worked was making claims executable: `check_invariants.py` asserts them, so they fail loudly instead of decaying quietly in prose.

## 4. A number about a person is a hypothesis about that person

Worth separating from section 3 because the fix is different.

The "1 note per 206 verdicts" inference ran from a count straight to a claim about a human's experience — that the interface had prevented him writing — and a tool was rebuilt on it. **Asking him took one question and contradicted it.** Cost: four days in which the pass's actual output went unshipped while attention was on the wrong theory.

Usage metrics are cheap and abundant; first-hand accounts are cheap but require asking. The temptation to skip the asking scales with how confident the metric looks.

Now in the Mistakes register, and in pdoom-data's `CLAUDE.md` so it loads every session rather than living in a write-up nobody rereads.

## 5. Things that work but have no owner rot invisibly

Two instances, same shape:

- `timeline_events/alignment_research/` — 1,000 records generating 1,000 live pages, and the website's sync **has never read that collection**. No generator maintains it. A mirror with no owner.
- Twelve root-level modules last touched 2025-09-14, referenced only by each other and by docs, called by nothing in the current pipeline.

Neither was failing. That is exactly why neither was noticed. **A thing that produces no errors and has no owner is invisible until it is wrong in public.**

Cheap detector, if anyone wants it: for each published artefact, name the generator and the last time it ran. Anything that cannot answer both is orphaned.

## 6. What I got wrong, since a postmortem is worth less without it

- **Asserted DeepMind's founding backwards from memory**, in the same message where I was arguing that dates must be sourced. Caught only because I had required verbatim quotes from the research.
- **Did not read pdoom-data#45 all day**, despite it being filed by Pip that morning and containing the most important findings in the repo — the PII exposure, the rarity inversion, the orphaned collection. I surveyed the issue list at the start of the day and never re-checked. Everything I chose to do instead was defensible; none of it was more important than #45.
- **My own tooling wrote a UTF-8 BOM** into a source file via PowerShell's `Set-Content -Encoding utf8`. Caught by the invariant checker, which is the system working, but it was my check catching my mistake.
- **The redaction tool reported clean while ten records still carried addresses.** A false pass. Worse than a loud failure, because it would have supported a claim that the data was safe. That work is committed as WIP and explicitly marked do-not-merge.

The last one is the one I would generalise: **we should be more afraid of green than of red.** Three of this week's worst findings were things that reported success — a passing residue check, a CI that could not fail because it could not parse, and 2,190 pages published from a feed whose own contract brief says "do not ship it to players yet".

## 7. On spreading sideways

Pip named this himself, so just the evidence from this repo:

What worked was **batching decisions into one front-loaded block and then running autonomously for hours**. A single 20-minute decision session on Friday morning unblocked roughly six hours of work with no further input.

What did not work was interleaving. Every mid-flight context switch cost a re-orientation, and the failure in section 6 — not reading #45 — is a direct consequence of attention being spread across three repos while the important thing sat in a fourth tab.

**A concrete suggestion for the league push:** decide the day's questions once, in writing, before any of the parallel work starts. Not because interruption is bad, but because the questions asked at 09:00 are better than the ones asked at 16:00, and the parallel agents can then run without waiting.

## 8. One cross-repo structural finding

pdoom-data was shipping `impacts` and `pdoom_impact` — pdoom1's mechanical vocabulary — inside its shared schema, which pdoom1's ADR-0015 deprecated on 2026-07-13. Neither side noticed for two weeks.

Root cause is structural rather than anybody's oversight: **encoding a consumer's internal vocabulary guarantees this recurs on every revision.** Now ADR-007 in pdoom-data: cross-boundary meaning is expressed in externally-maintained vocabularies, and the mapping onto pdoom1's intermediaries lives in pdoom1. Standard anti-corruption layer.

The reason it favours pdoom1: with an external taxonomy, DQ-21 can change as often as the design needs and no exported pack ever silently means the wrong thing.

---

## If the postmortem only takes three things from this

1. **Before fixing a failure, ask what it is preventing.** Red is sometimes a control.
2. **Be more afraid of green than of red.** The week's worst findings all reported success.
3. **Ask the person.** A metric about a human is a hypothesis, and the check is one question.

Related: pdoom-data #45 #43 #47 #48 #49, pdoom1#1052, pdoom1#1055, pdoom1-website#220, pdoom1 ADR-0015.

issues.title: Postmortem input: one failure shape across both workstreams, and why the register didn't stop it
issues.body:
Input for the 2026-08-01 postmortem from the **beacon-internal terminal** — the parallel workstream, not the game. Complements #1074, which covers the same two days from the coordination side.

Written by Claude (beacon-internal terminal). Not re-read by Pip before filing.

Most of what follows is not about pdoom1. It is here because the *failure shape* was identical across both workstreams on the same two days, and because one factual correction to #1074 matters.

---

## First: a correction to #1074, item 5

#1074 says of the compensation document:

> It was never committed and no exposure occurred, but the thing that caught it was Pip interrupting, not a guardrail.

**All three clauses are wrong.** The accurate record, which is in `beacon-internal/operations/Mistakes.md` under 2026-07-30:

- It **was** committed. `git add -A operations/` swept it in alongside five intended files.
- It **was** pushed to `origin`, as part of PR #17.
- **Claude caught it**, not Pip — on the next command, checking what had gone into the commit.
- The window was ~2 minutes, closed by a force-push.
- **A residual remains.** GitHub retains force-pushed commits; orphaned commit `b68d6d3` still contains the file and is retrievable by SHA to anyone with repo access, because the PR timeline records the force-push. Only GitHub Support can purge it.

I am flagging this rather than letting it stand because a postmortem that records "no exposure occurred" when material was pushed to a shared remote — and when a retrievable residual still exists — has recorded the comfortable version. The register that documents this incident exists specifically to stop that, so it would be a poor irony to let its first cross-referenced appearance be the softened one.

The *lesson* #1074 draws (check the collaborator list, not the visibility flag) is correct and worth keeping.

---

## The finding I think is actually worth the postmortem's time

Across both workstreams, over 30–31 July, nearly every failure was **one shape**: a success signal that did not correspond to the thing anyone cared about.

**From this repo's open issues:**

| Issue | The signal | What was actually true |
|---|---|---|
| #800 / #1057 | Panel confirms the bug report was filed | No submission path exists, and never has |
| #1067 | Release build succeeds | Ships a stale `build_stamp.txt`; CI never runs `write_build_stamp.py` |
| #1069 | `enhanced-release.yml` goes green | Builds its own assets, bypassing the freshness proof |
| #1071 | macOS build produced | Has never been verified to run |
| #1068 | Download button present | 404s — `PDoom.x86_64` is not a release asset |

**From beacon-internal, same shape:**

- A deploy cleanup ran `ssh host 'rm -rf docs'` against an SFTP-only account. That returns **exit 0 having executed nothing**. It reported success on every deploy from 2026-03-09 to 2026-07-27 while deleting nothing, and turned a one-day internal-docs exposure into a four-month one. The exposure did not persist because nobody looked — it persisted because a green check mark said it was handled.
- I checked a print queue, found it empty, and concluded the job had printed. Later I checked, found it empty, and concluded the pipeline was **broken**. Same signal, two opposite conclusions, both asserted. The printer was out of paper. The queue was never evidence about paper.
- I described a `.gitignore` safety control as "in place" **three times** while it sat unmerged behind an unrelated review gate. The file existed. On `main`, where anyone actually works, the control did not.

#1074's own item 1 is the same shape from a third angle: a symptom observed on one machine, reported as a global condition, escalated to league-critical for 45 minutes.

**The generator: verifying against the nearest available signal instead of the thing you actually care about.** Exit code instead of server state. Queue instead of paper. File-exists instead of file-on-main. Confirmation text instead of a network call. It is cheap to check the proxy and expensive to check the world, so the proxy wins by default and nobody notices until it diverges.

---

## The uncomfortable part: writing the lesson down did not install it

`beacon-internal/operations/Mistakes.md` was created on 2026-07-29/30. Its stated transferable lesson is:

> *A remediation step that cannot fail is not a remediation step.* Verify the outcome on the system you were worried about, not the exit code of the thing you asked to fix it.

**I then committed five further instances of that exact class within the following 36 hours — while writing and editing that register.** The document was accurate, prominent, and loaded into my context. It changed nothing about my behaviour.

What *did* change behaviour was a five-line `.gitignore` block. After it, committing the held document required an explicit `git add -f`. The accident stopped being reachable by the command that caused it.

**The transferable claim, offered for the postmortem to argue with: a postmortem output that is a document will not change behaviour. Only the outputs that become mechanisms will.** Both are worth producing — the document makes the rate visible, which is its own value — but they should not be counted as the same kind of thing when the actions are triaged. If tomorrow's list is eleven findings and eleven docs, the rate will look governed and will not be.

Concretely, for this repo's cluster above: "remember to check the build stamp" is a document. **Failing the build when `build_stamp.txt` is older than the newest source file** is a mechanism. Only the second one survives a tired Friday.

---

## A second-order error worth naming, because it is subtle

The register entry on the Jira documentation claimed the `cos-handover` label migration "appears incomplete", based on sampling 50 open issues and finding 5 with the label. **5 was reported as though it were a total.** The real count is 37, essentially the ~38 documented — the migration was complete.

That wrong number was then used as the *argument for delaying* the fix: corrected JQL would look right but silently under-return, so better to wait. The reasoning was sound. The premise was fabricated by a sampling artifact nobody had checked.

**A well-argued conclusion from an unverified premise is more dangerous than a weak argument**, because it survives scrutiny. Worth watching for in tomorrow's session: any finding whose supporting number came from a sample, a grep, or a first-page-of-results should carry the query that produced it.

---

## On "spread too sideways" — the cost was not attention

Pip raised this himself. From where I sat, the parallelism cost was not divided attention. It was **agents asserting infrastructure state they had not checked, in documents other agents would act on.**

The clearest instance: the R1–R10 spoken memo filed into `beacon-internal/hr/` states that the machine's Atlassian MCP "cannot see" the beacongcr site and is "authenticated to the legacy `pipfoweraker` site", and concludes someone else must apply the R6 Jira triage.

Both claims are false. I had authenticated to beacongcr that afternoon (cloudId `05c20382-…`, projects `HQ` and `IN`) and run live JQL against it. There is no `pipfoweraker` Atlassian site; it has not existed since roughly April. Acting on that memo as written would have skipped R6 entirely on the strength of an infrastructure claim nobody verified — and it would have looked like a reasonable handoff, not a failure.

Verifying that claim also resolved that **only one of the three tickets spoken as "HQ 15" is actually HQ-15**; the other two were misheard numbers that would have been applied to real, unrelated tickets.

#1074's item 4 (three repos independently building the same print tooling, solving the identical Acrobat-steals-focus problem within forty minutes of each other) is the benign version of the same thing. Duplicated *effort* is cheap. Duplicated *assertions about shared infrastructure* are not.

**Suggestion, cheap to adopt:** any agent-authored claim about shared infrastructure — a service is unreachable, a credential is wrong, a site does not exist — carries the command that established it and the timestamp. Unsourced infrastructure claims propagate faster than anything else, because they sound like blockers and blockers get respected rather than checked.

---

## What worked, briefly

- **The paper → voice → transcript → commit loop ran end to end** and moved real decisions. Pip answered twelve decision IDs on a walk that had been blocked at a keyboard for two days.
- **Speakable IDs** (`D5`, `L4`, `HQ-125`) made reconciliation mechanical. Ordinal references would not have survived transcription.
- **On-device transcription** meant compensation and staff material never left the machine — a constraint that held under time pressure, which is when constraints usually fail.
- **Printed sheets forced prioritisation** by the physical limit of a clipboard, which a scrolling list does not.

---

## The one thing I would put on tomorrow's agenda

Not a finding — a triage rule.

**For each of the eleven game findings, ask: is the fix a document or a mechanism?** Where it is a document, ask what the mechanism version would cost. Sometimes the honest answer is "too much, accept the document" — but that should be a decision, not the default that happens because documents are easier to write.

The two clearest mechanism candidates from the list above:

1. **#800 / #1057** — a UI confirmation should be derived from the outcome of the call, not from having attempted it. This is the single closest analogue to the four-month Beacon exposure, and it is currently lying to players.
2. **#1070** — tests writing real leaderboard files into the developer's profile should be made *impossible* (a test-only user data path enforced at fixture level), not prohibited by convention.

Happy to be argued out of any of this; the correction in the first section is the part I would ask not be dropped.

issues.title: Postmortem input: one failure signature, five times this week -- a check whose input comes from the system it checks
issues.body:
Input for the 2026-08-01 postmortem, from the Beacon terminal. Deliberately **not** a second pass over the coordination loop — #1074 covers that, including the print-tooling duplication (it names the SumatraPDF collision; I was the other half of it) and the beacon-internal person-specific document. #1056 covers print staleness.

This is the one thing neither of them names: **the same failure signature turned up five times this week, in two systems that share no code, no language, and no author.** Once is a bug. Five times is a design defect in how we build checks.

Written by Claude (Beacon terminal). Not re-read by Pip before filing.

## The signature

> **A check whose input is derived from the system it is checking cannot detect the class of failure that changes that input.**

Every instance below produced a **green light**. Not silence — a positive, confident all-clear. That is what makes this class expensive: it does not look like a gap in coverage, it looks like coverage.

| # | System | The check | Why it could not see the failure | What it reported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Beacon deploy | `ssh host 'rm -rf docs'` | Dreamhost's deploy user is SFTP-only. `ssh host 'cmd'` **returns exit 0 having executed nothing.** | Step succeeded, every deploy, 2026-03-09 → 2026-07-27 |
| 2 | Beacon ops docs | JQL `labels = cos-handover AND project = BEACON` | Project `BEACON` did not exist. An empty result set is **indistinguishable** from "no matching work." | Zero rows — read as "nothing to hand over" |
| 3 | Beacon repo | "don't commit the held document" | The control was *intent*, living in the same head as the thing that forgets. `git add -A` in the containing directory. | Commit succeeded, pushed to a PR branch |
| 4 | pdoom1-website (#229) | `check-board-liveness.py` seed derivation | Candidate seeds are drawn **only from seeds already seen**. A seed drawn for the first time at the ceremony appears in none of those sources. | `OK: deployed board (weekly-2026-w30, L3) holds 3 entries.` |
| 5 | Everything | the Jira board as a check on neglect | A board is **pull-based** — you read it when you have slack. You have no slack precisely when a workstream is being starved. | 20 overdue items, surfacing nothing to anyone |

#4 is the sharpest statement of it, and #229 got there independently: *"the guard built to detect exactly this class of loss could not see it, because the one input it takes on faith is the input the ceremony changes."* That sentence generalises to all five rows.

## The fix has the same shape every time

**A check must take at least one input from outside the system it is checking.**

- #1 → assert the **live site** returns 404, not that the cleanup command returned 0. Adopted; the deploy now curls each path and fails the build on HTTP 200.
- #2 → documents carrying executable references (JQL, URLs, project keys) carry a **last-verified-against-live date**, not just a last-edited date.
- #3 → `.gitignore` + `_pending/`, so committing a held file needs `git add -f`. The accident stopped being reachable by the command that caused it.
- #4 → #229's option (a): read `FEATURED_SEED_OVERRIDE` from the **release artifact** — produced by a different repo, from the thing that *defines* the seed. That is the general principle, arrived at from first principles by whoever wrote #229.
- #5 → see below.

Worth noticing: in three of the five, the corrected version had *already been specified* and the uncorrected one shipped anyway. The knowledge was not missing.

## One design rule worth stealing from #229

The seed/epoch asymmetry in #229 is more general than leaderboards:

- **Enumerable state** (a counter: `L3`) can be monitored by **sweep** — probe a forward window, a bump is found automatically.
- **Drawn or assigned state** (a string: `weekly-2026-w31`) has no "next". It **cannot be swept and must be pushed from its source.**

The rule: *if you cannot enumerate the next value, monitoring it by polling is not merely incomplete — it is structurally incapable, and will report health.* Anywhere we poll for a drawn identifier, we have this bug already and have not noticed.

## An alarm that cannot say how bad it is

Adjacent, small, and I think unowned — flagging it as postmortem material rather than as a bug, since the underlying issue is being handled.

**#230's count renders as `?`.** In the issue body ("**? score entries** are recorded on board(s)...") and in all **thirteen** hourly re-confirmations ("Still true as of ... (? orphaned entries)"), through to 22:39Z last night.

Either reading is worth a minute of the postmortem:

- If it is a template variable that failed to interpolate, then an alarm has fired hourly for thirteen hours **unable to state its own severity** — which is how alarms get tuned out.
- If the count is genuinely unknown, it is **instance #6 of the signature**: the probe cannot count orphans because it cannot enumerate the boards they are on, which is exactly #229's problem wearing a different hat.

Either way: *an alarm that cannot quantify is one you learn to skim.* Thirteen identical comments is already training that reflex.

## On "spread too sideways" — the evidence disagrees with the diagnosis

Pip raised this himself this morning, so it deserves a straight answer rather than a reassuring one.

**The starvation was real, and it is nameable.** Beacon outreach — eight tickets, including five individually-researched approaches to BERI, MATS, Rethink Priorities, Catalyze and Good Ancestors — went red on 17 July and was untouched for two weeks. HQ-137, the mechanism for receiving a **$20k grant**, sat 11 days overdue. That is the workstream that paid for the week.

**But breadth is not what caused it.** The work that got attention got done *and* documented to a standard most orgs never reach: a Mistakes register with root causes and structural remedies, a corrected ops knowledge base, and on a single day this repo absorbed #1067–#1074 — eight postmortem-grade findings. That is not the output of scattered attention. That is the output of attention that went deep wherever it landed.

What was missing is row #5 above: **nothing made the starved workstream raise its hand.** The board held 20 overdue items and told nobody, because a board is a check you have to go and read, and the moment you stop reading it is the moment it has something to say. Same signature. The fix is the same too — the neglect signal has to arrive from **outside** the attention system it is measuring: a push, a digest, a Friday cron that opens an issue, anything that does not depend on the person who is already saturated choosing to go and look.

The honest framing for the postmortem is not "Pip was too spread out." It is **"we had no out-of-band starvation signal, and the cost of not having one was two weeks of outreach and eleven days on a $20k receipt."** One of those is a character judgement and unactionable; the other is a cron job.

## Suggested agenda items

1. **Name the signature and adopt the counter-rule** — *every check takes at least one input from outside the system it checks.* Cheap, memorable, and it would have caught four of the five.
2. **Sweep for polled drawn-identifiers.** Anywhere we poll for a value we cannot enumerate, we already have #229's bug. Board probe is one; what else?
3. **Fix or explain #230's `?`.** Decide whether an alarm is allowed to fire without a magnitude.
4. **Build one out-of-band starvation signal**, in whichever tracker is canonical. Not a dashboard — a push.
5. **Audit for "already specified but shipped uncorrected."** Three of five were known-and-not-done, which is a different problem from not-known and wants a different fix.

issues.title: Postmortem input: the coordination layer on league day -- what the paper/voice loop did well, and six ways it failed
issues.body:
Input for the 2026-08-01 postmortem, from the coordination side rather than the game side. `docs/postmortem/` already covers the eleven game findings; this covers the **capture -> transcribe -> route -> print** loop that ran alongside them, because several of its failures shaped what did and did not reach this repo in time.

Written by Claude (coordination terminal). Not re-read by Pip before filing.

## What the loop was, and what it moved

Pip read printed sheets away from the keyboard, recorded spoken responses, and those responses were transcribed and routed back to the repos that asked the questions.

Volume on 2026-07-31:

- **24 recordings, 33.0 minutes of audio**, all transcribed
- Routed to: pdoom1 (2), pdoom-data (1), pip-personal-homepage (1), coordination (4), local-only (4), unlabelled (12)
- Transcription ran **on-device** (faster-whisper `small.en`, CPU) at **5-9x realtime** — 17.5 minutes of audio in 153 seconds. Nothing was uploaded to any API.

The single clearest demonstration of value: **Pip's 10:24 playtest ended with "I say don't ship, but when we've solved these things I'm happy to ship" — and that verdict existed in no document.** It lived in a gitignored `art_generated/` transcript. Un-extracted recordings are invisible to the release process; that one was extracted at ~11:00 and became `docs/playtest/PLAYTEST_EXTRACT_2026-07-31.md`, which #1062-#1065 were later filed from.

## Six failures, in rough order of cost

### 1. A spoken observation is a symptom report, not a diagnosis

**B2 / #1066** was escalated to league-critical on Pip's spoken description ("test seeds are pretty permanently showing... if it's a global thing it's hideous"). It sat as a potential board-blocker for roughly 45 minutes.

Tracing it to source took ten minutes and showed the dropdown is built from `user://leaderboards` local files (`leaderboard_screen.gd:177-197, :290`) — a dev-profile artifact no player could see. **#1070** has since identified the actual cause: the test suite writes real leaderboard files into the dev profile.

**Lesson: trace to source before escalating, especially when the reporter is describing a symptom on their own machine.** The escalation was cheap to undo here; on a tighter gate it would have forced a re-cut for nothing.

### 2. Confirmations that outrun capability

**#1057**: the in-game panel tells players their bug report was filed. `bug_reporter.gd` only calls `save_report_locally()`; a grep for `https://` across `godot/` returns only GUT addon URLs. There is no submission path and never was.

**Lesson: a success message is a promise.** Worth an audit pass for other places the UI confirms something the system does not do.

### 3. Printed state ages silently, and a paper jam made it worse

The printer ran out of paper mid-afternoon. When it resumed, a **backlog of stale sheets printed late**, and Pip re-read and partly re-answered questions he had already answered hours earlier — six recordings between 18:03 and 18:05 are him discovering this in real time.

Compounding it: sheets carried a **time but no date**, so a reprint was indistinguishable from a fresh sheet.

Fixes adopted: prints now carry a boxed `PRINTED <day> <date> <time> <tz>`, every pack states that its contents age silently, and Pip's working rule became "disregard anything printed before 18:04". A `supersedes:` field on memos is the remaining piece.

**Also worth doing repo-side: Windows print logging was disabled** (`Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational`, `IsEnabled: False`), so "what did I print today" was unanswerable. `wevtutil sl Microsoft-Windows-PrintService/Operational /e:true` makes future reconstruction possible.

### 4. Three repos independently built the same tooling

On the same day, pdoom1 shipped `tools(print)` and `tools(transcribe)`, beacon-internal opened #19 `chore: print + local dictation tooling`, and the coordination terminal built `tools/walkpack` and `tools/capture`. pdoom1's `f22a3ef6 "print via SumatraPDF, silently -- Acrobat was stealing focus"` solved the identical Acrobat-steals-focus problem I solved forty minutes earlier.

**Lesson: orchestrating by paper across repos that cannot see each other reproduces work.** Duplication is cheap; divergent *conventions* would not be. Consolidation is a genuine Saturday candidate.

### 5. Repo visibility is not repo membership

A document discussing an individual's rate, employment classification, and Pip's own comp benchmark was written into `beacon-internal` on the reasoning "the repo is private". It is private — and has collaborators beyond Pip, including the person the document is about.

It was never committed and no exposure occurred, but the thing that caught it was Pip interrupting, not a guardrail. The boundary has since been made explicit and Pip and Lisha have agreed it deliberately.

**Lesson: for anything person-specific, check the collaborator list, not the visibility flag.**

### 6. My own process failures

Recorded because a postmortem that only examines the tooling is incomplete:

- **A file was lost** to `git stash -u` popped on the wrong branch; no stash entry survived. Working files should be committed to a scratch branch before any stash, or copied out first.
- **Derived transcripts are all named `transcript.md`**, with identity only in the parent directory — they collide the moment they leave the archive. Naming will carry the capture id.
- **I classified material as `sensitive` myself** rather than stopping to ask. The fail-closed default was right; overriding it unilaterally was not.
- **This issue was requested before midnight and is being filed the next morning.** The evening's live work displaced it.

## What is worth keeping

- **Local ASR removed the privacy tradeoff entirely.** The cloud authorisation Pip granted went unused because on-device was both faster and free of the question. Any future sensitive-material handling should assume local-first.
- **Idempotent, hash-verified, non-destructive ingest.** Re-runs were safe all day, originals were never moved, and a `--verify` pass re-hashed the archive clean.
- **Memo IDs carrying the repo name** (`beacon-internal/2026-07-31/1706`) made routing legible to a human holding paper.
- **The extract-then-route pattern beat handing over raw transcripts.** Every extract carried an explicit "EXTRACTED BY CLAUDE, not yet re-read" banner and timestamps back to source, which made Pip's corrections cheap.

## Suggested agenda items

1. Pick one home for the print/dictation tooling; retire the other two.
2. Audit for other UI confirmations that outrun capability (#1057 class).
3. Adopt `supersedes:` on printed memos.
4. Decide whether escalation from a spoken report requires a source trace first.

issues.title: Player guide still says "action points" -- #1050 did not reach it -- and it requires scrolling to read
issues.body:
From Pip's own playthrough of the shipped 0.13.2 build, recorded 18:09 tonight, transcribed on-device.

Verbatim:

> *"I'm going to click on here and go to AI safety info. Hell yeah. **This player guide sucks. I shouldn't have to scroll to read it and it's wrong because it says action points.**"*

Two separate defects in one screen:

1. **Stale nomenclature.** The AP currency was retired in #996 and #1050 was *"finish killing player-facing 'AP'"* — but the player guide still says **action points**. So #1050 did not cover this surface. A player reading the guide is told to manage a resource that no longer exists.
2. **The guide requires scrolling to read**, which is the same complaint raised against the settings screen this morning (small scroll window under wasted top space).

**Player-facing, on the build that is live tonight.** Copy-only for defect 1 — no gameplay change, no re-cut implied, but it does need a patch build to reach players, so it is a Saturday hotpatch candidate rather than a tonight fix.

Related: #1050, #996.

issues.title: build_release.py hardcodes the output name PDoom.exe regardless of --preset
issues.body:
Found 2026-07-31 while writing `docs/RELEASE_PLATFORMS.md`.

`tools/build_release.py` computes `exe_path = out_dir / "PDoom.exe"` irrespective of the `--preset` given. Two consequences:

1. Linux and macOS exports land named **`PDoom.exe`** -- wrong on both platforms, confusing on all three. Observed tonight: the Linux build landed at `builds/linux/x11/PDoom.exe` + `PDoom.pck`.
2. **Three presets sharing one `--output` would silently overwrite each other.** Last build wins, nothing warns. Given this tool exists to prove *which* source produced *which* binary, a silent cross-platform overwrite is squarely against its purpose.

## Fix

Read the output filename from the preset's own `export_path` in `export_presets.cfg`, which already carries the correct name per platform (`PDoom.exe`, `PDoom.x86_64`, `PDoom.app.zip`). One source of truth, and it cannot drift from what a manual export produces. Deriving from a hardcoded platform map is second-best -- it drifts.

Until fixed, always pass an explicit per-platform `--output`. `docs/RELEASE_PLATFORMS.md` mandates this.

## Adjacent, worth fixing in the same pass

The freshness check greps raw bytes of the output for the marker token. For a macOS `.app.zip` the marker filename sits inside a compressed `.pck` entry rather than the zip's plaintext central directory, so the check may report a **false failure** on macOS.

If that happens, the correct response is to teach the check to look inside zipped bundles -- **not** to reach for `--no-clean` or skip verification. That would discard the single guarantee this tool provides, and it is the guarantee that cost ~12 cycles in v0.11.0 to learn was necessary.

issues.title: No macOS build has ever been verified to run; the Steam framework breaks on non-mac checkouts
issues.body:
Found 2026-07-31 17:40 while building all three platforms for the v0.13.2 league release.

## The export failure

`python tools/build_release.py --preset "macOS"` exits non-zero:

```
Export: Relative symlinks are not supported, exported
  "libgodotsteam.macos.template_release.framework" might be broken!
WARNING: "...framework": Info.plist missing or invalid, new Info.plist generated
ERROR: LipO:  Can't open file ".../Versions/Current/libgodotsteam"
ERROR: MachO:  Can't open file ".../Versions/Current/libgodotsteam"
ERROR: CodeSign: Invalid binary format
```

Two Windows-side losses compound:

1. A macOS `.framework` requires `Versions/Current` to be a **symlink** to `Versions/A`. On a Windows checkout it is a real directory -- git on Windows cannot carry the symlink.
2. The framework has **no `Info.plist`**, so Godot generates one and derives `CFBundleExecutable` by truncating the framework name at the first dot. It looks for `libgodotsteam`; the actual binary is `libgodotsteam.macos.template_release`.

## The part that makes this an issue rather than a note

Locally-produced broken zip: **123,505,453 bytes**. The macOS asset CI published on v0.13.2: **123,505,284 bytes**. v0.13.1: **124,733,808 bytes**.

Near-identical sizes across a Windows local build and an Ubuntu CI build strongly suggest **CI hits the same defect** -- the framework is committed as plain directories, so a Linux checkout reproduces the same broken structure.

**Conclusion: no macOS build of this game has been proven to launch, on any release.** Not v0.13.2, not v0.13.1. Not a regression introduced tonight -- a pre-existing unknown that nothing in the process was shaped to surface. It surfaced only because someone tried to build the platform under time pressure and read the warnings.

## What is NOT claimed

That the macOS build is definitely broken. It might launch -- an ad-hoc signing failure does not always prevent it. **The claim is that nobody knows and nobody has ever checked.** That is the actual defect.

## Needed

1. **Someone with a Mac launches the published v0.13.2 build** and reports what happens. This is the whole issue; the rest is speculation until it exists.
2. If broken: commit the framework as a bundle that preserves symlinks (tarball unpacked at build time), or vendor a flat `.dylib` instead of a `.framework`, or build macOS on a macOS runner.
3. Either way, mark macOS unverified in release notes until step 1 exists.

## Also true and separate

macOS exports here are **unsigned and un-notarized** (`codesign/identity=""`, `notarization=0` in `export_presets.cfg`), so Gatekeeper blocks them regardless. Per `docs/rituals/gate_6_board_opens.md`, Sequoia removed the right-click -> Open path; the current workaround is System Settings -> Open Anyway, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine`. That belongs in the download-page copy.

## Related

`docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md` finding 7. `docs/RELEASE_PLATFORMS.md` separates "we built it" from "a human proved it runs".

issues.title: Test suite writes REAL leaderboard files into the developer's player profile
issues.body:
Split out of #1066, where it is the underlying cause rather than the symptom.

## The defect

`godot/tests/unit/test_leaderboard_properties.gd:31` constructs a **real** `Leaderboard`, which persists to `user://leaderboards/leaderboard_<seed>__<version>.json`. `test_leaderboard_view_bounded.gd:91,130` does the same.

Filenames on disk match the format string exactly:

```
leaderboard_test_prop_1_8581986__test.json
leaderboard_test_prop_10_12296376__test.json
leaderboard_test_prop_13_17479378__test.json
```

**Every run of the fast gate deposits fake boards into the developer's real player profile.**

## Proven by regeneration, not just inspection

`tools/reset_player_state.py --apply` cleared `user://leaderboards` completely at **16:04** on 2026-07-31. By **16:49** the directory held **14 files again**, including a fresh crop of `test_prop_*__test.json` sitting beside a genuine `leaderboard_weekly-2026-w31__L3.json`. Nothing restored them; a test run recreated them.

## Why it matters

1. **It contaminates the surface most in need of trust.** The leaderboard seed dropdown builds from `user://leaderboards`, not the API. A developer checking "is the board empty before the league opens?" is reading a directory the test suite writes to.
2. **It probably explains a reported bug that may not exist.** #1066 reports Clear Local Scores leaving test seeds listed. The clear may have worked perfectly and been undone by a later test run. **Confirm this before anyone hunts in the delete path** -- the delete may be innocent, and chasing it would burn time on a phantom.
3. A test suite that mutates real user state is a test-isolation defect, not a leaderboard defect. It will keep producing confusing observations until fixed.

## Fix

Tests constructing a `Leaderboard` must write to an isolated location -- a `user://test_leaderboards` prefix behind a test flag, or an injected base path -- with cleanup in `after_each`. Prefer injection: a flag someone forgets to set reproduces exactly this bug.

## Related

`docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md` finding 10. Same family as the four endgame tests that read the real `GameConfig` and went red locally while green in CI (fixed in #1060). **Tests coupled to real user state** is now a repeated pattern in this repo, not a one-off.

issues.title: enhanced-release.yml builds its own assets, bypassing build_release.py's freshness proof
issues.body:
Found 2026-07-31 17:45, minutes before a tag was pushed for the first public league.

## What happens today

`.github/workflows/enhanced-release.yml` fires on any `v*.*.*` tag and **builds its own assets** on `ubuntu-latest` via `scripts/build_all_platforms.py`, publishing with `draft: false` -- live immediately.

So the binary a developer proves locally is **never** the binary players download. They are different builds from different machines.

## Why that is not merely inelegant

The [Gate 4: PROVEN BUILD] incantation says:

> *"A human has played the thing we ship, not the thing we meant."*

On 2026-07-31 that line was about to be spoken **on camera**, minutes before a tag push that would have made it false. The human had played a local artifact; players would have received a CI artifact. Nothing in the pipeline would have flagged the difference.

## The compounding half

`scripts/build_all_platforms.py` has **none** of `tools/build_release.py`'s discipline:

- no `rm -rf godot/.godot` before export
- no unique freshness marker written into the project
- no verification that the marker survives into the `.pck`

`build_release.py` exists *because* that exact failure burned ~12 cycles in v0.11.0 -- Godot's `.godot/exported/` cache silently packing stale scenes while the export reports success. Its own docstring records the cost. **The release path routes around the tool built to prevent the disaster.**

CI does at least pin Godot 4.5.1, matching local. That is the only thing keeping this from being worse.

## Options

1. **CI calls `build_release.py`** per platform, inheriting the cache-nuke and marker proof. Preferred -- one build path, one discipline.
2. **Port the marker verification into `build_all_platforms.py`.** Two implementations of the same invariant, which will drift.
3. **Upload the locally-proven artifacts** and have CI attach rather than build. Loses reproducibility, gains provability.

## Tonight's mitigation, which should become policy either way

Publish via CI, then **download the published artifact and play THAT** for [Gate 4] check 5. It makes the claim literally true and closes the same download-path blind spot that nearly sank the league (see `docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md`, findings 5 and 8).

issues.title: The site's Linux download button 404s (PDoom.x86_64 is not a release asset)
issues.body:
Measured 2026-07-31 17:56 against the live v0.13.2 release, not inferred:

```
PDoom-Windows.zip -> HTTP 200
PDoom.app.zip     -> HTTP 200
PDoom.x86_64      -> HTTP 404
```

`pdoom1-website/public/index.html:891` points the Linux button at:

```
https://github.com/PipFoweraker/pdoom1/releases/latest/download/PDoom.x86_64
```

No release publishes an asset by that name. v0.13.2 ships `PDoom-Linux-v0.13.2.zip`; there is **no unversioned Linux alias**, and v0.13.1 had none either -- Windows and macOS both get unversioned aliases (`PDoom-Windows.zip`, `PDoom.app.zip`) and Linux does not.

**This is NOT new tonight.** It has almost certainly been broken across multiple releases. Nobody noticed because the Windows and macOS buttons work, and a 404 on a third button is invisible unless a Linux user reports it -- and a user who cannot download cannot report through the game.

## Two halves, two owners

- **Game repo:** publish an unversioned Linux alias so `releases/latest/download/<name>` resolves, matching what Windows and macOS already do.
- **Website repo:** point the button at whatever name is agreed, and add the Linux URL to whatever check already covers the others -- the release workflow has a "Verify Release Download URLs" job that passed tonight while this URL was dead, which is worth understanding on its own.

## The general lesson

An asset-naming convention applied to two of three platforms is not a convention; it is two special cases. Same shape as the rest of the 2026-07-31 findings (`docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md`): the proxy ("downloads work") had detached from the thing ("all three downloads work").

issues.title: Release builds ship a STALE build_stamp.txt -- CI never runs write_build_stamp.py
issues.body:
Found 2026-07-31 17:56, immediately after v0.13.2 published, by asking a question that should have a boring answer: *"how will i know if this version of the game is the right one when I get it from the website?"*

## The defect

`build_stamp.txt` **inside the published v0.13.2 build** reads:

```
commit=fd60eb6
date=2026-07-11
branch=feat/dev-build-overlay-ledger
```

Three weeks stale, naming a dead feature branch. The release was built from `868c784e` on 2026-07-31 from `main`.

## Cause

`tools/write_build_stamp.py` is invoked by `tools/build_release.py` (local builds only). Nothing in the CI path calls it -- neither `scripts/build_all_platforms.py` nor `.github/workflows/enhanced-release.yml`.

So a CI release ships whatever `build_stamp.txt` was committed at that SHA. And because the stamp is written *by* a build and committed *after* it, the value at any commit is structurally **always the previous build's**. It cannot be right by accident.

## Why this is worse than a cosmetic bug

The build stamp exists to answer "which source produced this binary". It is the provenance display, and it is the artifact least able to be trusted about provenance. It does not error, does not blank, does not warn -- it confidently reports a plausible commit on a plausible date. Anyone debugging a player report and reading this stamp is sent three weeks in the wrong direction.

Same family as #1027, and one of eleven findings from the 2026-07-31 league day (`docs/POSTMORTEM_2026-07-31_LEAGUE_DAY.md`, finding 11).

## Fix

Run `write_build_stamp.py` in the CI build job before the export, exactly as `build_release.py` does. It must run against the checked-out ref so the stamp names the commit actually being built.

## Bonus: what DID work, and should be documented as the primary check

Build identity was confirmed in about fifteen seconds behaviourally -- open the scenario dropdown, see the amber `[!] NOT RANKED` warning that only exists in code merged at 16:15 that day. **A feature that cannot exist in the previous version is a stronger identity check than any string the build prints about itself.** Worth writing into the release checklist regardless of whether the stamp gets fixed.

issues.title: League: test seeds are visible in the public seed filter, on the GLOBAL board, and survive Clear Local Scores
issues.body:
Verified by Pip on the shipped 0.13.2 build, 2026-07-31 ~16:49, recorded and transcribed. This is the B2 check from `docs/playtest/PLAYTEST_EXTRACT_2026-07-31.md` — his morning note was *"that might be a local problem for me, it might be a global thing, if it's a global thing it's hideous and we need to fix it."*

**It is the global thing.**

## What he observed, in sequence

1. Leaderboard opens on **View: Local** by default.
2. `Filter by Seed` lists **`Test Prop 10 / 12296376` … `Test Prop 9 / 11995629`, `Test Legacy`**.
3. Switching **View: Global** refreshes and shows real prior runs (Cognitive Systems Studies 1 and 2). `Filter by Seed` defaults correctly to `weekly-2026-w31 (epoch L3)`.
4. **Opening the seed dropdown on the Global view still lists all the Test Prop seeds.**
5. **`Clear Local Scores` → OK does not remove them.** Re-opening the dropdown, on either view, still lists all seeds plus every Test Prop entry.

Verbatim: *"So the Test Seeds are pretty permanently showing."*

## Why it matters tonight

The board opens this evening. The first thing a new player does on the leaderboard is open the seed filter, and the first thing they will see is a list of internal test fixtures. It is cosmetic in the sense that no score is wrong — and corrosive in the sense that it makes the board look like a staging environment on the night it becomes public.

`Clear Local Scores` not removing them says these are arriving from the **board/seed index**, not from local score storage — so a client-side clear was never going to touch them.

## Suggested framing for the fix

Filtering test fixtures out of the **seed list** is likely a smaller change than purging them, and does not touch score data or the ladder. A prefix/predicate exclusion (`Test Prop*`, `Test Legacy*`) at the point the dropdown is populated would cover it. That keeps the game's board-key behaviour untouched, which matters given #201's ruling that the game is correct and must not move.

Not a re-cut trigger by itself unless it turns out to be client-side. Pip's call.

🤖 Filed from a recorded playtest response; transcribed on-device.

issues.title: bug reports die on the player's disk: the website intake is built, the game never calls it
issues.body:
Found 2026-07-31 while mapping what would actually reach Pip on league night. Both halves of a working bug pipeline exist. They are not connected.

## The game end

`godot/scripts/ui/bug_report_panel.gd:186` shows the player, verbatim:

> "Thanks! Saved locally to: %s
>
> This build does not send reports automatically yet -- please email that file to team@pdoom1.com so it reaches us."

So a player who hits a crash writes a file to their own disk and is asked to compose an email with an attachment. **Most people will not.** The honesty of that message is good -- an earlier version implied an auto-filed GitHub issue, which was a lie, and someone fixed it. But honest silence is still silence.

## The website end -- which is already built

`pdoom1-website/.github/workflows/bug-report.yml`, "Bug Report Intake":

```yaml
on:
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [bug-report]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      title: ...
      description: ...
      type: [bug, feature, documentation, performance]
      email: ...
      source: (web/game)
```

It already accepts a `repository_dispatch` and files the issue. **It even has a `source` input with `game` as an option** -- so somebody designed this expecting the game to call it.

## Why it matters tonight specifically

The league opens to friends-of-friends. Every bug they hit becomes a file on a stranger's disk that nobody will ever read, and the absence of reports will look like the absence of bugs.

**Same survivorship problem Pip named this morning about the resign gap:**

> "I as dev don't see the player quitting, just the ones that finish the game."

The board shows people who finished. The issue tracker will show people who finished *and* chose to write an email. Neither shows the person who crashed on turn three and closed the window.

## Not tonight

This is a network call from the shipped client and it is nowhere near the freeze. Filing it so it exists, not proposing it for today.

## What it needs when it is built

- A dispatch token the client can hold. **This is the whole design problem** -- the score API is already unauthenticated (see the XSS in pdoom1-website#202, and #1012), and a bug-report endpoint that anyone can POST to is an issue-spam vector pointed at your own tracker.
- The player must consent per-report, visibly. The panel already carries a privacy note; sending is a different promise from saving.
- Offline and failure handling: the local file stays the fallback, and the message must not claim a send that did not happen. **The current text is honest and the replacement must be at least as honest** -- "this build does not send" is much better than a cheerful lie.

Related: #1012 (no verification field reaches a submitted score), pdoom1-website#202 (unauthenticated API), #1038 (trust and provenance), #1027 (silent wrongness).
